sections.title: Basic Concept of Cause and Effect
sections.content: Cause and Effect means reason and result. A Cause is an event that makes something happen, and an Effect is the result that occurs because of that cause. Example: It rained heavily, so the road was flooded. Here rain is the cause and flooding is the effect.

sections.title: Direct Causation
sections.content: In direct causation, one event directly produces another event. There is a clear relationship between the two events and the result appears immediately. Example: The electricity went off, so the room became dark. Here the power outage directly causes darkness.

sections.title: Common Cause
sections.content: Sometimes two different events appear related but both are actually caused by a third event. This is called a common cause. Example: People are carrying umbrellas and traffic is slow on the road. The reason for both could be rain.

sections.title: Independent Causes
sections.content: In independent causes, two events are not related to each other. Each event occurs due to its own separate cause. Example: One student is studying and another student is playing cricket. The causes of both events are different.

sections.title: Clues to Identify Cause and Effect
sections.content: Certain words often indicate cause and effect such as: because, therefore, as a result, due to, hence. If one event logically follows another, it may be the effect.

sections.title: Types of Questions Asked in Exams
sections.content: 1. Identify which statement is the cause and which is the effect. 2. Determine whether both events are caused by the same reason. 3. Decide whether the events are independent or logically connected.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Assuming causation just because events occur in sequence. 2. Creating a relationship between two events too quickly. 3. Failing to identify a common cause. 4. Incorrectly linking independent events.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: A Cause is an event that produces a result. An Effect is the outcome that occurs after the cause. The three main types are Direct Causation, Common Cause, and Independent Causes. While solving questions, always focus on the logical relationship between events.

tricks.title: Cause Comes Before Effect Rule
tricks.explanation: Usually the cause happens first and the effect follows. If event A happens before event B and there is a logical relationship, A may be the cause.
tricks.example: A holiday was declared at school, so students went home.

tricks.title: Ask the 'Why' Question
tricks.explanation: Whenever you see a result, ask yourself why it happened. The answer you find will likely be the cause.
tricks.example: The road is wet → Why? → It probably rained.

tricks.title: Common Cause Identification Trick
tricks.explanation: If two different events occur together, check whether a third factor might be affecting both.
tricks.example: People carrying umbrellas and wet roads → Cause: Rain.

tricks.title: Identify Independent Events
tricks.explanation: If there is no logical relationship between two events, they may have independent causes.
tricks.example: One person is drinking tea and another is buying a mobile phone.

tricks.title: Recognize Signal Words
tricks.explanation: Words like because, therefore, as a result, and due to often indicate cause and effect.
tricks.example: The match was canceled due to heavy rain.

tricks.title: Immediate Result Identification
tricks.explanation: If one event instantly produces another event, it is likely direct causation.

tricks.title: Check the Time Gap
tricks.explanation: If two events occur with a logical time connection, they may form a cause–effect relationship.
tricks.example: The alarm rang and the person woke up.

tricks.title: Avoid Unrelated Events
tricks.explanation: Do not assume every two events form a cause and effect relationship. First check if a real connection exists.
tricks.example: A student is studying and it is raining outside → both are independent.

tricks.title: Simple Logic Rule
tricks.explanation: If event B seems impossible without event A, then A may be the cause.
tricks.example: There is no electricity, so the fan is not working.

tricks.title: Avoid Overthinking
tricks.explanation: Level 1 questions usually involve everyday logical relationships, so use simple reasoning to answer them.
tricks.example: There is a traffic jam because road construction is going on.
